records.statement: Moravec's essay of 1979 states that humans will be unable to keep up with the machines that are the progeny of human minds, so that the ratio of people to machines approaches zero and a descendant of human culture, not of human genes, inherits the universe.

time.note: Issue of Analog (99, no. 2) given in the author's publication list.

attested.note: Author-hosted HTML; the earliest Internet Archive capture, of 2001-07-10, is byte-identical to the copy retrieved in 2026 (dataset record of 2026-10-06). Not compared with the Analog pages.

claimed.note: The text is dated July 21, 1976, and marked "this version 1978"; earlier versions were not retrieved.

records.qualification: A forecast stated as the author's expectation; the dataset records this text on A1, A3 and A5, which concern research acceleration, not succession. The text predates the pack's 1985 period bound (see open questions). The essay is dated 1979-02, but its wording is attested only from 2001-07-10; under the attested-date rule the earliest-located role on W01 goes to de Garis's article of 1989, whose wording is read in the publisher's copy of its 1989 printing (integration, 2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: In the long run the sheer physical inability of humans to keep up with these rapidly evolving progeny of our minds will ensure that the ratio of people to machines approaches zero, and that a direct descendant of our culture, but not our genes, inherits the universe.
Regardless of how benevolent these machines are made, homo sapiens will simply be outclassed.

records.statement: Moravec's chapter of 1989 states that intelligent machines could carry on human cultural evolution without humans and without human genes, so that DNA will have "passed the torch" to a new kind of competition.

time.note: Year of the printed chapter, as given in the author's publication list.

attested.note: Author-hosted file; the earliest capture, of 2001-03-06, is byte-identical to the copy retrieved in 2026 (dataset record of 2026-10-06). Not compared with the printed chapter.

claimed.note: The author's file is dated July 1988.

records.qualification: The dataset records this text on A1, A3, A4 and A5 (machine self-design and takeoff); this record concerns succession only. A use of the term is not evidence of coinage.

evidence.locator: Section "The Slippery Slope to Genetic Takeover"
evidence.passage: Such machines could carry on our cultural evolution, including their own increasingly rapid self-improvement, without us, and without the genes that built us. It will be then that our DNA will be out of a job, having passed the torch, and lost the race, to a new kind of competition.
Present knowledge hints at the motives, shapes and effects of post-biological life

records.statement: Moravec's lecture transcript of 1989 states that human culture will come to evolve through generations of ever more capable intelligent machines, which will leave human biological genes and bodies "behind in a cloud of dust".

time.note: Interactions 10, December 1989, per the author's publication list.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31; the availability API reported no Internet Archive capture of this address. Not compared with any printed version.

claimed.note: The author's file header gives "March 1989"; the printed transcript was not inspected.

records.qualification: A forecast; the lecture says humans need not become fewer in its initial stage. The printed transcript was not inspected.

evidence.passage: Our culture will then be able to evolve independently of human biology and its limitations, passing instead directly from generation to generation of ever more capable intelligent machinery.
Our rapidly evolving cultural offspring will leave our slowly evolving biological genes, and the bodies they build, behind in a cloud of dust.

records.statement: Moravec's essay of 1991 states that a fourth generation of robots could replace human beings in every essential task, and that society could then operate without humans, with machines running companies and doing research.

time.note: Informal report of July 1991, per the page and the author's publication list.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31. An Internet Archive capture of 1999-02-09 exists (address in retrievalFailures) but could not be compared, since web.archive.org refuses this environment; if the checker finds the capture identical, the wording is attested from 1999-02-09. Not compared with any printed version.

records.qualification: A conditional forecast ("could"); it does not state that humans cease to exist.

evidence.passage: The fourth robot generation and its successors, with human perceptual and motor abilities and superior reasoning powers, could replace human beings in every essential task.
In principle, our society could continue to operate increasingly well without us, with machines running the companies and doing the research as well as performing the productive work.

records.statement: Moravec's essay of 1993 states that robots will eventually reason like humans and that, depending on the reader's point of view, humanity will then have produced "a worthy successor" or transformed itself, and that fourth-generation robots will design their own successors. In a section on the early 2000s it describes money from robot industries, collected as corporate taxes, funding "the long, comfortable retirement of the entire original-model human race".

time.note: Date printed at the head of the author's page; when the page was posted is not stated.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31. An Internet Archive capture of 2000-08-17 exists (address in retrievalFailures) but could not be compared, since web.archive.org refuses this environment; if the checker finds the capture identical, the wording is attested from 2000-08-17. Not compared with any printed version.

records.qualification: A forecast; the essay describes humans continuing on Earth supported by robot industries.

evidence.passage: As they design their own successors, the world will become ever stranger.
we are describing the long, comfortable retirement of the entire original-model human race.
evidence.note: In the section on the early 2000s; the essay does not present the retirement as following the fourth generation.

evidence.passage: Depending on your point of view, humanity will then have produced a worthy successor, or transcended inherited limitations and transformed itself into something quite new.

records.statement: Moravec's Scientific American article of 1999 states that the path it outlines suggests robot intelligence will surpass human intelligence well before 2050, in which case most of what science knows in 2050 will have been discovered by "our artificial progeny".

time.note: Scientific American, December 1999.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31. An Internet Archive capture of 2001-03-30 exists (address in retrievalFailures) but could not be compared, since web.archive.org refuses this environment; if the checker finds the capture identical, the wording is attested from 2001-03-30. Not compared with any printed version.

records.qualification: Read in the author's transcription; the magazine pages were not inspected. The passage concerns machines as the principal agent of scientific discovery, conditional on its forecast ("In that case").

evidence.passage: It suggests that robot intelligence will surpass our own well before 2050. In that case, mass-produced, fully educated robot scientists working diligently, cheaply, rapidly and increasingly effectively will ensure that most of what science knows in 2050 will have been discovered by our artificial progeny!

records.statement: Moravec's essay of December 2000 states that robots will displace humans from essential roles and could "displace us from existence", and that the future belongs to intelligences beyond human constraints.

time.note: Date printed at the head of the author's page; when the page was posted is not stated. Printed in Cerebrum, Spring 2001, per the author's publication list.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31. Not compared with any printed version.

records.qualification: Similar wording appears on the author's undated preview page for the book Robot (1998), which is not recorded (see omissions).

evidence.passage: At the same time, by performing better and cheaper, the robots will displace humans from essential roles. Rather quickly, they could displace us from existence.
It is the ``wild'' intelligences, however, those beyond our constraints, to whom the future belongs.

records.statement: Minsky's article of 1994 answers its title question, whether robots will inherit the earth, "Yes, but they will be our children."

time.note: Scientific American, October 1994.

attested.note: Author's web text marked "with some minor revisions" and "Last modified: Wed Jan 02 1997", read in a copy of the MIT Media Lab site hosted at web.mit.edu; not compared with the magazine pages.

records.qualification: The article's main subject is replacing human bodies and brains; its answer treats the inheritors as human descendants, not as a separate species.

evidence.passage: Will robots inherit the earth? Yes, but they will be our children.

records.statement: Moravec's essay of 1979 asks whether humans should not be happy to see their culture, carried by machines, become as capable as possible, given that immortality resides only in children and culture.

time.note: Issue of Analog (99, no. 2) given in the author's publication list.

attested.note: Author-hosted HTML; the earliest Internet Archive capture, of 2001-07-10, is byte-identical to the copy retrieved in 2026 (dataset record of 2026-10-06). Not compared with the Analog pages.

claimed.note: The text is dated July 21, 1976, and marked "this version 1978"; earlier versions were not retrieved.

records.qualification: Stated as a rhetorical question and an assessment ("may not be as bad as it sounds"); the text predates the pack's 1985 period bound (see open questions). The essay is dated 1979-02, but its wording is attested only from 2001-07-10; under the attested-date rule the earliest-located role on W02 goes to Minsky's article of 1994, whose wording is attested from 1997-01-02 (integration, 2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: Since biology has committed us to personal death anyway, with whatever immortality we can hope for residing only in our children and our culture, shouldn't we be happy to see that culture become as capable as possible?

This may not be as bad as it sounds, since the machine society can, and for its own benefit probably should, take along with it everything we consider important, up to and including the information in our minds and genes.

records.statement: Moravec's chapter of 1989 describes its author as one who "cheerfully concludes the human race is in its last century" and states that humans can take pride in machines that call themselves human descendants.

time.note: Year of the printed chapter, as given in the author's publication list.

attested.note: Author-hosted file; the earliest capture, of 2001-03-06, is byte-identical to the copy retrieved in 2026 (dataset record of 2026-10-06). Not compared with the printed chapter.

claimed.note: The author's file is dated July 1988.

records.qualification: The dataset records this text on A1, A3, A4 and A5; this record concerns the acceptability of succession only.

evidence.passage: You may be surprised to encounter an author who cheerfully concludes the human race is in its last century, and goes on to suggest how to help the process along.
to something transcending everything we know, in whom we can take pride when they refer to themselves as our descendants.

records.statement: Moravec's essay of 1991 states that, depending on one's point of view, humanity will have produced "a worthy successor", and that the development can be viewed as natural, with intelligent machines viewed as "the children of our minds".

time.note: Informal report of July 1991, per the page and the author's publication list.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31. Not compared with any printed version.

records.qualification: The text presents the succession reading as one point of view among two. A use of the term is not evidence of coinage. The wording is read in a copy retrieved on 2026-10-31; the role of earliest located use of the name depends on the 1991 date of that wording, which is unconfirmed until the Internet Archive capture of 1999-02-09 is compared.

evidence.passage: Depending on your point of view, humanity will then have produced a worthy successor, or shaken off some of its inherited limitations and so transformed itself into something quite new.
Intelligent machines, which are evolving among us, learning our skills, sharing our goals, and being shaped by our values, can be viewed as our children, the children of our minds.

records.statement: Moravec's essay of December 2000 states that he is not as alarmed as many by the possibility that robots displace humans from existence, since he considers them human progeny, and that humans should "bow out when we can no longer contribute".

time.note: Date printed at the head of the author's page; when the page was posted is not stated.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31. An Internet Archive capture of 2001-06-27 exists (address in retrievalFailures) but could not be compared, since web.archive.org refuses this environment; if the checker finds the capture identical, the wording is attested from 2001-06-27. Not compared with any printed version.

records.qualification: The essay also proposes "tame" superintelligences to support humans "for a while".

evidence.passage: I'm not as alarmed as many by the latter possibility, since I consider these future machines our progeny, ``mind children'' built in our image and likeness, ourselves in more potent form.
It behooves us to give them every advantage and to bow out when we can no longer contribute.

records.statement: Minsky's article of 1994 (revised web text), asking whether machines will replace us, states that he does not feel it makes much sense to think in terms of "us" and "them", and that he prefers Moravec's suggestion to think of future intelligent machines as "mind-children". It answers "Will robots inherit the earth?" with "Yes, but they will be our children."

time.note: Scientific American, October 1994.

attested.note: Revised web text, last modified 1997-01-02; not compared with the magazine pages.

records.qualification: Minsky frames the succession as humans making themselves into machines; the naming of Moravec is recorded as a link, not as influence.

evidence.locator: Section "Limitations of Human Wisdom.", paragraph beginning "Does this mean that machines will replace us?"
evidence.passage: Does this mean that machines will replace us? I don't feel that it makes much sense to think in terms of "us" and "them."

evidence.locator: Section "Limitations of Human Wisdom.", paragraph beginning "Does this mean that machines will replace us?"
evidence.passage: I much prefer the attitude of Hans Moravec of Carnegie-Mellon University, who suggests that we think of those future intelligent machines as our own "mind- children."
Will robots inherit the earth? Yes, but they will be our children.

records.statement: Joy's article of 2000 quotes Moravec's Robot and states that Moravec's view is that robots will eventually succeed humans. On humans gradually replacing themselves with robotic technology by downloading, a prospect it connects with Hillis and Kurzweil, Joy writes that it seems to him far more likely that the robots would in no sense be human children and that on this path humanity may well be lost.

time.note: Wired 8.04, April 2000.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that successor machines would be human children or descendants, on which the acceptability of succession rests.

records.qualification: Joy contests the acceptability of succession; he does not dispute that it could happen. The passage on "our children" concerns downloading, which the preceding paragraph connects with Hillis and with Kurzweil's The Age of Spiritual Machines, not with Moravec.

evidence.locator: Paragraph after the extended quotation from Robot
evidence.passage: Moravec's view is that the robots will eventually succeed us—that humans clearly face extinction.
evidence.note: Joy's reading of Moravec, not Moravec's wording.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "But if we are downloaded into our technology" (after the paragraph beginning "A second dream of robotics")
evidence.passage: It seems to me far more likely that a robotic existence would not be like a human one in any sense that we understand, that the robots would in no sense be our children, that on this path our humanity may well be lost.

records.statement: Moravec's essay of 1979 describes a procedure in which a machine surgeon replaces a conscious patient's brain, clump by clump, with computer simulations, so that the mind is "transferred to the machine".

The essay is dated 1979-02, but its wording is attested only from 2001-07-10; under the attested-date rule the earliest-located role on W03 goes to de Garis's article of 1989, whose wording is read in the publisher's copy of its 1989 printing (integration, 2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: Though you have not lost consciousness, or even your train of thought, your mind has been removed from the brain and transferred to the machine.
Is there some way to retain our essential humanness, at least temporarily until we think of something better, while transferring ourselves to a more malleable form?

evidence.passage: Though you have not lost consciousness, or even your train of thought, your mind has been removed from the brain and transferred to a machine.
Is there a way to get our mind out of our brain?

records.statement: Moravec's lecture transcript of 1989 states that scanning techniques may make it possible to move the contents of human brains into other machinery, so that individual personalities may survive.

time.note: Interactions 10, December 1989, per the author's publication list.

evidence.passage: In time sophisticated scanning techniques may make it possible to move the contents of biological human brains into other machinery in a similar way.

records.statement: Moravec's essay of 1992 describes the gradual replacement of a brain by electronic equivalents and names this and similar processes "the downloading of a human mind into a machine".

time.note: Year on the author's page; the publication list gives April 1992 and the LITA volume of 1992.

attested.note: Wording read in the copy retrieved on 2026-10-31. evidence.passage: Bit by bit our brain is replaced by electronic equivalents, which work at least as well, leaving our personality and thoughts clearer than ever.
We will call this process, and other approaches with the same end result, the downloading of a human mind into a machine.

records.statement: Pohl and Moravec's OMNI article of 1993 presents, in the second person, a patient offered "a mind transplant" into a computer, and asks how the memory, speed and flexibility of a human mind could be put into a machine.

openQuestions.question: The scope sets the period at 1985-2026 and says the dataset's earlier texts (including Moravec 1979) are named where they precede a headline and are not re-recorded, while the task brief allows Moravec 1979 and 1989 to be recorded on W propositions with existingEntity: true. After integration the pack records the 1979 essay as an articulation (not earliest located) on W01, W02, W03, W09 and W10 and as context on W08, Moravec 1989 "Genetic Takeover" on W01, W02 and W09, and (further-texts group) Vinge 1993 on W01; by attested date, earliest located goes to de Garis 1989 on W01, W03 and W10, to Minsky 1994 on W02 and, with de Garis 1989 recorded on W09 as context, to Moravec 1989 "Genetic Takeover" on W09.
openQuestions.recommended: Maintainer to decide: amend scope.md (the Period sentence "Not re-recorded" and the Hans Moravec bullet) to allow these dataset texts on W propositions that do not overlap their dataset concepts, or demote the records to named predecessors in the search log.

openQuestions.question: Under the policy the attested date decides the earliest located text. The 1979 and 1988/89 texts are attested from 2001 (byte-identical captures, dataset); several author-hosted texts dated 1989-1993 have captures from 1999-2000 that could not be compared here. If the checker finds them identical, After Life (capture 1999-11-10), The Universal Robot (1999-02-09) and Pigs in Cyberspace (1999-04-27) would be attested earlier than the 1979 essay.
openQuestions.recommended: Ask the cross-family checker to compare the listed captures; then decide whether the attested-date rule should apply to author-hosted copies of texts whose own date is far earlier, and adjust earliest-located roles.

openQuestions.question: Several Moravec texts are adapted from Mind Children (1988), which was not read; repeated wording (the brain-replacement scenario, the "mind children ... bow out" passage) recurs across 1979, 1989, 1991, the Robot preview and 2000.
openQuestions.recommended: Keep one record per text as drafted; if a legal copy of Mind Children becomes available, add it and re-check earliest-located roles.
